title: Runway Incursion Avoidance
summary: Know where every part of the aircraft is, what movement is authorized, and when to stop and clarify.
objectives: Recognize runway boundaries, signs, and lighting without relying on habit.
Separate taxi routing, crossing, line-up, and takeoff permissions.
Maintain a clear airport-position model before departure and after landing.

sections.title: The protected area and the whole airplane
sections.body:
A runway incursion involves an incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or person in the protected area used for landing and takeoff. The hazard extends beyond an aircraft sitting on the painted runway surface. A wingtip or tail extending across a holding boundary can intrude while the cockpit appears clear.

Before taxi, locate the departure runway, expected route, crossings, and published hot spots on a current airport diagram. A hot spot flags a place with a history or potential for confusion or collision; it is a reason to prepare for the specific geometry, not a separate clearance. Know how a runway change would alter the plan.
sections.deep:
Why: the pilot sees from one point in an aircraft with a large footprint. Holding-position markings and protected areas preserve space for arriving or departing traffic, including wing and obstacle clearance. Treat the airplane’s position as a physical envelope rather than the location of the nosewheel or a moving-map dot.

Scenario: the next intersection looks familiar, but its sign differs from the diagram you expected. Stop where safe before entering an uncertain area. Ask for clarification or progressive taxi instructions. Continuing a few more feet to discover where you are can consume the protected separation you were trying to preserve.

sections.title: Signs, markings, and lighting as cross-checks
sections.body:
A runway holding-position marking has two solid and two dashed yellow lines. Approaching from the solid side, remain behind it until authorized to enter or cross at an airport with an operating tower. Stop so that no part of the airplane extends past the boundary. A runway hold sign uses white characters on red. A taxiway location sign has a black background with yellow identification; direction signs use yellow with black information.

Use the sign, pavement marking, diagram, and surrounding geometry together. A single clue is less reliable in darkness, rain, glare, or construction. Yellow guard lights draw attention to a runway boundary. They do not supply a clearance.
sections.deep:
Why: independent visual cues reduce the risk of recognizing the right shape at the wrong location. A runway number can be checked against a heading indication before departure, but magnetic indication alone does not prove the correct parallel runway. Verify the full runway designation and the actual pavement.

The dashed side generally faces the runway being exited. Crossing that boundary while leaving the landing runway is different from crossing another runway ahead. An ILS critical-area hold marking and an intersecting-taxiway hold marking have different designs and purposes. Learn each as a distinct instruction rather than labeling every yellow line “the runway.”

sections.title: A taxi route does not authorize every runway movement
sections.body:
A taxi instruction identifies a destination and route. It does not by itself authorize entering the departure runway or crossing every intervening runway. Obtain explicit permission for each runway crossing and for runway entry. A clearance to cross a runway is not a takeoff clearance. Line up and wait permits positioning on the specified runway and waiting; it does not permit beginning the takeoff roll.

Write the clearance, identify each limit on the diagram, and read back runway assignments, runway crossings, and hold-short instructions with the aircraft identification. Listen for the controller’s correction. If the transmission is incomplete, blocked, or ambiguous, ask again before moving into the uncertain area.
sections.deep:
Why: errors often begin when a pilot hears the expected route rather than the actual instruction. Reading back while locating each named taxiway checks both memory and interpretation. At a boundary, compare the instruction you actually received against the sign immediately in front of you.

Practice: give the learner a changed route with an intermediate hold short. Ask the learner to point to the limit and explain what further authorization would be needed. Do not reward a fast readback if the student cannot locate the clearance boundary. If an instruction appears unsafe or conflicts with a visible hazard, communicate the conflict promptly.

sections.title: Taxi workload and non-towered operations
sections.body:
Taxi is an active flight-safety task. Finish programming and lengthy checklist discussion while stopped in a suitable place. Keep the cockpit focused on movement, traffic, routing, and instructions. Brief passengers before taxi so that a request for quiet during a busy intersection is expected rather than abrupt.

At a non-towered airport, no ground controller supplies runway separation or authorizes your crossing. Review the airport information and traffic direction, monitor the appropriate frequency, announce relevant intentions, and visually check the runway and approach areas before entering. Radio silence and a self-announcement are both insufficient proof that the runway is safe.
sections.deep:
Why: taxi combines steering, braking, clearance interpretation, radio monitoring, and an unfamiliar visual scene. A moving map can help orientation, but heads-down fixation and inaccurate position display can create a new hazard. Maintain enough speed margin to stop before a hold boundary, obstacle, or developing conflict.

At an airport with a closed tower, confirm the published procedures and airspace status rather than assuming daytime tower procedures still apply. Teach the student to state what evidence supports a runway entry: known position, a suitable traffic picture, visual checks, and compliance with the applicable procedures. A transmission reports intent; it does not force other traffic to yield.

sections.title: The runway is not clear until the tail is clear
sections.body:
Before landing, brief likely exits and any adjacent runway. After landing, maintain control and clear the landing runway using an appropriate exit. The aircraft is not clear until all parts are beyond its applicable holding-position marking. Crossing that marking must not carry the aircraft into another runway’s protected area without the required authorization.

Once safely clear, obtain or follow the applicable taxi instruction. Avoid stopping on the runway to change frequencies or perform an after-landing checklist. Equally, do not accept a hurried exit that exceeds safe turning or braking capability. If there is insufficient space between boundaries, tell ATC rather than guessing which runway area may be occupied.
sections.deep:
LAHSO: land-and-hold-short operations require the pilot to understand the stopping point and available landing distance, assess actual performance, and explicitly accept or decline the clearance. The FAA advises student pilots and pilots unfamiliar with LAHSO not to participate. A pilot may decline an unsafe or unsuitable offer.

Why: after touchdown, workload falls just as vigilance often relaxes. Nearby parallel or intersecting runways make a successful landing followed by a wrong turn entirely possible. Continue the positional cross-check until parking, including the location of the entire aircraft and each remaining clearance limit.

sections.title: Night, low visibility, and runway status lights
sections.body:
Darkness and poor visibility reduce the distance at which signs, painted lines, and vehicles can be recognized. Taxi more slowly as needed, use an airport diagram, and identify a boundary early enough to stop. Lighting patterns help orientation, but a blue edge light or green centerline alone does not establish which taxiway you occupy. Avoid lighting that blinds another pilot or obscures your own view.

Runway status lights independently warn of detected conflicts. Illuminated red runway entrance or takeoff hold lights mean an unsafe condition exists. Remain stopped or stop safely as appropriate, and advise ATC when the indication conflicts with an instruction.
sections.deep:
Why: the surveillance-based warning is a safety layer separate from the controller’s clearance. The controller may not be able to see the activation directly. Lights going out do not authorize entry, crossing, or takeoff; the applicable ATC clearance is still required.

If already in a dynamic situation where stopping would itself be unsafe, use the safest aircraft-specific judgment and communicate promptly. Do not turn a simple “red means stop” teaching model into a demand for an unsafe high-speed action. The learner should understand both the warning’s meaning and the need to manage the actual aircraft state.

teachBack: Point to every runway crossing and hold boundary on a realistic taxi route, then explain what is and is not authorized.
Show where the tail must be before reporting clear of the landing runway.
A clearance conflicts with red runway entrance lights. Explain what you would do and what you would say.
takeaways: Use the entire aircraft footprint when holding short or clearing a runway.
Require explicit runway crossing and entry permission at an operating tower.
Line up and wait is not takeoff permission.
Dark runway status lights do not provide a clearance.

quiz.question: The nosewheel has crossed a runway exit holding-position marking, but the tail has not. Is the aircraft clear of the landing runway?
options: Yes, because the cockpit is on the taxiway.
Yes, if the next aircraft has not landed.
No, all parts must be beyond the applicable marking.
No, because an exit always requires another crossing clearance.
feedback: The pilot’s viewpoint is not the aircraft’s full footprint.
The position requirement does not depend on whether another aircraft has touched down.
The tail still occupies the protected side of the boundary.
Normal exit from the landing runway differs from entering or crossing another runway.
quiz.hint: Use the farthest part of the aircraft, not the nosewheel.

quiz.question: Ground assigns a route to Runway 27 that crosses Runway 18, but no crossing authorization is heard. What should the pilot do at Runway 18?
options: Cross because Runway 27 is the clearance destination.
Hold short and obtain explicit crossing authorization.
Cross after announcing on the ground frequency.
Enter Runway 18 and stop on its centerline.
feedback: A destination and taxi route do not independently authorize the intervening runway crossing.
The runway boundary remains a limit until the crossing is explicitly authorized.
An announcement is not a substitute for ATC authorization.
Crossing the hold boundary already creates the protected-area intrusion.
quiz.hint: Separate the route from permission to enter each runway.

quiz.question: Tower instructs the aircraft to line up and wait. The runway ahead looks clear. Which action is authorized?
options: Begin takeoff after a final scan.
Begin takeoff when the preceding airplane rotates.
Cross the opposite hold line to leave the airport.
Enter the assigned runway, align, and wait for further instructions.
feedback: A clear visual scene does not create a takeoff clearance.
Traffic progress does not convert line-up permission into takeoff permission.
The instruction does not authorize an unrelated runway crossing or taxi route.
Line up and wait allows positioning but requires waiting for a takeoff clearance.
quiz.hint: Identify the action the instruction explicitly withholds.

quiz.question: An aircraft is holding at illuminated red runway entrance lights despite having heard a crossing clearance. What is the appropriate response?
options: Remain stopped and ask ATC to resolve the conflict.
Cross because a verbal clearance overrides the lights.
Cross when the lights go dark without further confirmation.
Turn the transponder off so the lights stop responding.
feedback: The warning indicates a detected unsafe condition that should be resolved with ATC.
The red warning is an independent conflict indication and should not be ignored.
Extinguishing lights is not itself an ATC clearance or a resolution of an uncertain instruction.
Disabling surveillance does not remove the aircraft conflict.
quiz.hint: Treat conflicting safety information as something to resolve before entering.

quiz.question: At a non-towered airport, the frequency is quiet after your departure announcement. What does that establish?
options: The runway is reserved for your takeoff.
No aircraft are in the pattern.
Only that you have not heard a conflicting transmission.
A takeoff clearance equivalent to a tower clearance.
feedback: An announcement does not reserve runway use.
Aircraft may be nonradio, on another frequency, or not transmitting.
Silence is incomplete information, so visual checks and appropriate procedures remain necessary.
No ATC clearance is created by a self-announcement.
quiz.hint: Distinguish absence of a radio report from absence of traffic.

quiz.question: You reach an unfamiliar intersection and cannot reconcile the sign with the taxi diagram. What should happen before entering the uncertain area?
options: Continue until another sign confirms the location.
Stop where safe and request clarification or progressive taxi.
Follow the airplane ahead without checking its clearance.
Use more speed to minimize time near the runway.
feedback: Continuing may cross the very boundary whose location is uncertain.
Stopping preserves space and allows the position and instruction to be resolved.
Another aircraft may have a different destination or authorization.
More speed reduces stopping and interpretation time.
quiz.hint: Preserve the ability to stop outside a protected area.
